title: Working at the Monogram from 1913 and later jobs
summary: Austin recounts working at the Monogram theater from 1913, shows in New York, dance studio work, and her recent illness.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Well, I went to work at the Monogram in 1913. In 13? And I worked at 34th Street until they moved to 35th Street, and I moved there with him. That's the first time I went to New York, and I came right back and stayed down there when I worked there 25 years straight. And then I went to New York and started working for Herdic and Seaman. I was taking high fast shows, and I worked for Herdic and Seaman for a long time. And then I came, when I came home, my mother died in 31. So I just came on the stage. You stayed here then all that time? And I was working at a studio downtown. I knew you'd been, yes.
I knew John Steiner told me you were playing piano for a dance studio.

Yeah, Jimmy Payne. Then I worked for him 17 years. Yes, I knew you'd been there. And then I worked for another woman, a white woman who had a studio down there at Jackson Boulevard, 22, East Jackson. Oh, yes. And then I got sick. I was in the hospital for four or five months, and I came out. My sister just died in November, in April. She'd been there almost two years now. Well, she had been there two years. Yes, you think this is that you have. So I haven't been doing anything since my sister died. I just stayed home. My brother-in-law and I live here together. My sister's southern. But other than that, I've been doing pretty good. You're looking fine, really. I had all my teeth taken out and I just got my teeth back. And, well, I've been doing all right. So this author of the stuff that just put me down in the bed and I couldn't walk.
I went to see Ike Robinson who had played with Jolly Roll for a while, the banjo player. And his wife was having trouble with her teeth. But I had a nice interview. That was two days ago.
You knew Jolly Roll, didn't you?
